title: Sell Mineral Rights in Mississippi
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Mississippi | TMS & Legacy
metaDescription: Tuscaloosa Marine Shale acreage or Smackover, Norphlet legacy oil in Mississippi? We give you the honest read on each and a fair cash offer either way.
heroLead: A decade ago, southwest Mississippi looked like it might become the next big shale story. It didn't quite happen, and understanding why matters for anyone holding acreage there today.
intro: Around 2013 and 2014, operators moved into the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale across Amite, Wilkinson, and Adams counties with real ambition, drilling horizontal wells and hoping to replicate the success of plays like the Eagle Ford. The rock turned out to be more difficult and expensive to produce than hoped, and most companies scaled back or exited within a few years. If you signed a TMS lease during that window, you likely remember the excitement, and you may also remember how quietly it faded.

Further east, Mississippi's older story runs through the Smackover and Norphlet formations in counties like Jasper and Clarke, deep, often high-pressure oil and gas production that has been running for decades with far less fanfare but considerably more staying power than the TMS ever achieved.

sections.heading: Being Honest About the TMS
paragraphs: If you are holding Tuscaloosa Marine Shale acreage in Mississippi hoping for renewed large-scale drilling, the realistic picture is that most operators who tried the play have moved on, and there is no broad indication that is changing soon. That is not the answer every owner wants to hear, but it is the one that leads to a fair offer instead of one built on speculation.

If your acreage does have production history, even limited, we look at that actual record. If it is undeveloped or leased but never drilled, that changes the conversation to what the lease itself, rather than a producing well, might be worth.

sections.heading: Smackover and Norphlet: The Quieter, Steadier Story
paragraphs: These are deep formations, often produced through wells that were drilled decades ago and have settled into long, slow decline. Some of this production dates back to the mid-20th century, and interests have frequently passed through several generations of the same family since.

Because these are older leases in many cases, deduction language can vary more than you would see on a modern lease, so it is worth confirming exactly what your lease says about post-production costs before assuming your net check is calculated the same way a newer one would be.

sections.heading: What Your Statement Actually Tells You
paragraphs: The county and operator name on your check are the fastest way to know which situation you are in. Amite, Wilkinson, and Adams point toward the TMS; Jasper, Clarke, and similar east-central counties generally point toward Smackover or Norphlet legacy production.

If you are holding a lease with no production at all, that is worth mentioning when you reach out too, since an undeveloped leased interest is priced very differently than one with an actual payment history behind it.

sections.heading: Selling a Mississippi Interest, Developed or Not
paragraphs: For a producing Smackover or Norphlet interest, we build the offer from documented decline the same way we would anywhere else. For TMS acreage, whether producing, leased, or held-open, the conversation starts with an honest look at what is actually there rather than what the play was once expected to become.
Closing follows the standard path, a mineral or royalty deed and a title check through the chancery clerk's office in the county where the interest sits, typically wrapped up within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Is the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale being drilled in Mississippi right now?
faqs.answer: Activity has been minimal for years after most operators scaled back or exited the play in the mid-2010s due to difficult geology and high costs. There is no broad current drilling program in the play.

faqs.question: Can TMS minerals be sold when leased but not producing?
faqs.answer: Yes, though an undeveloped leased interest is valued differently than a producing one. We would look at your lease terms and any nearby activity rather than a production history that does not exist yet.

faqs.question: Why is your Smackover check so much steadier than what you hear about shale wells?
faqs.answer: Smackover and Norphlet production in Mississippi is largely decades-old, mature production that settled into a slow, predictable decline long ago, unlike a newer shale well still working through its steepest early decline.

faqs.question: How do you find out which county your Mississippi interest is in?
faqs.answer: Your royalty statement or lease should list the county and legal description. If you are unsure, send us what you have and we can help identify it from the operator and well information.

faqs.question: Will your TMS lease automatically renew if the operator never drilled?
faqs.answer: That depends entirely on the lease's specific terms, primary term length, delay rental or shut-in provisions, and whether any of those conditions were met. Reviewing the actual lease language is the only reliable way to know its current status.

faqs.question: Are Smackover and Norphlet the same formation?
faqs.answer: No, though they are often produced together in the same wells in parts of Mississippi. The Smackover is a limestone formation and the Norphlet a sandstone, sitting at different depths, and a single well can sometimes draw royalty from both.
